---
title: "Use it from Python"
subtitle: "An extra, about 20 minutes, at your own pace. Everything runs on your computer."
---

::: {.callout-note}
## What this is for

The model you set up answers your scripts the same way it answers the chat app. Your data stays on your computer,
there's no charge per use, and with two settings you can get the same answer every time. You need to have written a
little Python, and to have finished [Set up](setup.qmd).
:::

## 1. Check that Ollama is running {#running}

Ollama should be running (the llama icon is showing), and the starter model should be downloaded. In a terminal:

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
ollama list
```
:::

**It works when** the list includes `{{< var starter.name >}}`. If it doesn't, go back to
[Set up](setup.qmd#starter).

## 2. Set up Python with uv {#uv}

uv is one small tool that installs Python and the packages you need. It needs no admin rights. If you already have it
(`uv --version` prints a number), skip to the project folder.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Mac

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```
:::

### Windows

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
```
:::
:::

**Close the terminal and open a new one**, so it can find uv. Then make a project folder and add the Ollama package:

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv init --vcs none --no-package dss-ollama
cd dss-ollama
uv add ollama
```
:::

**It works when** the last command ends with a list of installed packages, including `+ ollama==0.6.3`. Save each
script below inside this folder.

## 3. Your first chat {#chat}

Save this as `hello.py`. It's the code from the slide.

```python
import ollama

reply = ollama.chat(model="gemma3:1b",
                    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}])
print(reply.message.content)
```

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv run hello.py
```
:::

**It works when** a greeting prints, like `Hello there! How's your day going so far?` The words will differ from
run to run. Step 5 fixes that.

## 4. Stream the answer {#stream}

Without streaming, nothing prints until the whole answer is done. With `stream=True`, you get it piece by piece, the
way the chat app shows it. Save this as `stream.py`:

```python
import ollama

stream = ollama.chat(model="gemma3:1b",
                     messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name three fruits."}],
                     stream=True)
for chunk in stream:
    print(chunk.message.content, end="", flush=True)
print()
```

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv run stream.py
```
:::

**It works when** the answer appears in pieces, for example a numbered list of three fruits.

## 5. Get the same answer every time {#repeat}

A model picks each word with a little chance. Two options remove it: `temperature` 0 means "always take the likeliest
word", and `seed` fixes whatever randomness is left. Save this as `repeat.py`:

```python
import ollama

for _ in range(2):
    reply = ollama.chat(model="gemma3:1b",
                        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name a fruit, in one word."}],
                        options={"temperature": 0, "seed": 42})
    print(reply.message.content)
```

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv run repeat.py
```
:::

**It works when** both answers match: `Apple`, then `Apple`. Take the options out and try again; the answers may
differ.

Repeatable also means writing down what you ran. Record these with your results:

- the model's **ID**, from `ollama list` (for `{{< var starter.name >}}` it's `97558784bdc9`). A name like
  `gemma3:1b` can point to a newer build later; the ID can't.
- the **Ollama version**, from `ollama -v`.
- the options (`temperature`, `seed`) and the exact prompt.

The same answer is guaranteed only on the same computer, with the same model and the same Ollama version.

## 6. A research-shaped example {#survey}

Label short survey answers by theme, one call each, and save a CSV. The model must pick from a fixed list. Save
this as `survey.py`:

```python
import csv
import ollama

themes = ["cost", "speed", "ease of use", "support", "other"]
answers = [
    "It took forever to load.", "I couldn't afford the license.",
    "The menus were confusing.", "Nobody answered my email for a week.",
    "Way too pricey for a student.", "Everything felt instant.",
    "I had to watch three videos to find the export button.",
    "The weather was nice that day.",
]
rows = []
for text in answers:
    prompt = (f"Label this survey answer with exactly one of: {', '.join(themes)}. "
              f"Reply with the label only.\n\nAnswer: {text}")
    reply = ollama.chat(model="gemma3:1b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                        options={"temperature": 0, "seed": 42})
    rows.append({"answer": text, "theme": reply.message.content.strip().lower()})
with open("themes.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["answer", "theme"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(rows)
```

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv run survey.py
```
:::

**It works when** a file named `themes.csv` appears in your folder, with one row per answer. Open it. On our test
run, the small starter model got seven of eight right. This is the wrong one:

```
The menus were confusing.,support
```

"The menus were confusing" is an ease-of-use answer, not a support one. A small model makes mistakes like this, and
these answers are made up, so never trust labels you haven't checked. Compare against labels you made yourself, and
try a bigger model by changing the name in the script. Your answers never left your computer.

## 7. Code 100 answers at once {#batch}

Step 6 coded eight answers. Research means hundreds. This script codes 100 made-up answers to "What would improve
your study experience at the Libraries?" into six themes, then checks itself against answers we coded by hand. Download
both files into your project folder:

- [survey-100.csv](downloads/survey-100.csv){download=""}: the answers, with our own coding on 20 of them.
- [code_answers.py](downloads/code_answers.py){download=""}: the script, about 60 lines. Open it and read it.

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv run --with ollama python code_answers.py survey-100.csv --model gemma3:4b
```
:::

One line counts up while it works (`coded 37/100 · 21 s`). Then it prints:

- **Themes:** how many answers landed in each theme, as a bar chart. Ollama's structured output makes every label one
  of the six, never a made-up seventh.
- **Agreement:** how many of our 20 hand-coded answers the model matched, and each one it didn't: our label, then
  the model's.
- **Time:** the total, and seconds per answer.
- **Fingerprint:** eight characters computed from all 100 labels. Run the script again with the same model: the same
  fingerprint means the same labels. It's step 5's `temperature` 0 and `seed`, at scale.

It also writes `coded.csv`, with one theme per answer.

**It works when** the last lines look like this. Your timing will differ, and your fingerprint may too: it
holds only on the same computer, model and Ollama version.

```text
The model agrees with our coding on 19 of 20.
  "I'd like a way to borrow laptops for a few days. Mine broke ..."
      ours: wifi and computers   model: seats and outlets

Total time: 95 s, 0.9 s per answer
Fingerprint of all 100 labels: 88bd5688
Run it again: same fingerprint, same labels.
```

Some honest notes:

- **The check matters more than the counts.** The chart looks convincing whatever the labels are. The agreement line
  is what tells you whether to believe it. Code a sample yourself first, as we did, and never trust labels you haven't
  compared.
- **Ambiguous answers are hard for people too.** About ten answers touch two themes. Our own pick is one defensible
  choice, not the truth.
- **Size matters.** With `gemma3:1b` on the same answers, the model agreed on only 12 of 20 and put nearly half the
  answers in "quiet space". Try it, then compare with `gemma3:4b`.
- **Speed depends on your computer.** On a Mac with a graphics chip, 100 answers take about a minute. On a laptop
  without a graphics card, `gemma3:4b` can take several minutes, so try `gemma3:1b` first. It's quick but less
  accurate.

## 8. Already have code for OpenAI's API? {#openai}

Ollama also speaks the same language as OpenAI's API. Point the `openai` package at your computer instead. Add it:

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv add openai
```
:::

Save this as `openai_hello.py`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")
reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gemma3:1b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
```

::: {.prompt .prompt-shell}
```bash
uv run openai_hello.py
```
:::

**It works when** a greeting prints. The key can be any text: Ollama doesn't check it, and nothing goes to OpenAI.
The only changes from code written for OpenAI are `base_url` and the model name.

## If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `ConnectionError: Failed to connect to Ollama. Please check that Ollama is downloaded, running and accessible.` | Ollama isn't running. Open the Ollama app and wait for the llama icon. With the `openai` package, the same problem reads `openai.APIConnectionError: Connection error.` |
| `ollama._types.ResponseError: model 'nope:1b' not found (status code: 404)` | The name is misspelled or the model isn't downloaded. Run `ollama list` and copy the name exactly, or run `ollama pull` for it. With `openai`, it reads `openai.NotFoundError: Error code: 404`. |
| `command not found: uv` (Mac) or `'uv' is not recognized` (Windows) | Close the terminal and open a new one. |
| The first call takes several seconds, later ones are quick | Ollama is loading the model into memory. It stays loaded for about 5 minutes after the last call. |
| A long run seems stuck | The model is working; a bigger model is slower. Use `stream=True` to watch it, and try a smaller model. |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ollama'` | Run the script with `uv run`, from inside your project folder. |

<p class="small-muted">Tested with Ollama {{< var ollama.checked >}}, Python package <code>ollama</code> 0.6.3,
<code>openai</code> 3.40.0 and uv 0.13.6, on Linux with {{< var starter.name >}} running on the CPU. Packages change
often; the <a href="https://github.com/ollama/ollama-python">ollama-python</a> page wins if something differs. Help
with your own setup: <a href="{{< var help >}}">go.ncsu.edu/getdatahelp</a>.</p>
